source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"APRNs have essentially the same regulated scope as registered nurses because advanced education and certification do not expand clinical authority.","B":"APRNs have an identical scope in every state because state practice laws do not affect independent practice or prescribing authority.","C":"APRNs are limited to tasks delegated to assistive personnel unless a physician is physically present for each clinical decision.","D":"APRNs are educated and certified to assess, diagnose, manage problems, order tests, and prescribe within authority granted in their jurisdiction."}}
source_row.rationale: NCSBN states that APRNs are educated and certified to assess, diagnose, manage patient problems, order tests, and prescribe medications, while regulatory authority can differ by jurisdiction. Option D is correct. Option A erases the advanced-practice role. Option B incorrectly claims state scopes are identical. Option C wrongly limits APRNs to assistive tasks and continuous physician presence.
source_row.source_detail: NCSBN — APRN Practice/Consensus Model: APRNs are educated and certified to assess, diagnose and manage patient problems, order tests and prescribe medications; practice and prescribing authority are governed by the jurisdiction where the patient is located and regulatory requirements vary among states/jurisdictions. Current NCSBN APRN practice guidance live-rechecked 2026-08-15; jurisdictional scope remains controlling and must not be generalized across all states. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: continuity/transfer of care, collaboration, legal/regulatory scope, quality improvement, leadership and professional-practice activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.stem: Which statement best describes the role of an advanced practice registered nurse (APRN) compared with a registered nurse in the United States?
